power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: How humans come to acquire language has been a persistent object of philosophical and scientific inquiry, in part because it bears on fundamental questions about the nature of human cognition.

Classically, this field of inquiry has centered innateness as a critical component of language acquisition, traditionally characterizing innate capability in terms of richly specified, biologically endowed linguistic structure, such as Universal Grammar.
Contemporary theories have evolved considerably from these earlier formulations and now present several differing candidates for innateness in language.

Throughout this evolution, though, questions of innateness have remained central to theories of language acquisition, even as the nature of those questions has shifted in response to new sources of evidence.

In this Perspective, we consider evidence from three complementary sources of evidence-linguistic diversity, human social interaction, and language models (LMs)-that together inform the question of what children must bring to the task of language learning.
We conclude by identifying desiderata for theories of language acquisition that seek to specify the nature, scope, and explanatory role of innate contributions to language development.
Communication through language is one of the most distinctive features of our species, and how humans acquire this capacity remains among the most enduring questions in the study of human nature.
Central to this inquiry is the concept of innateness, which has shaped theories of language acquisition for decades.

More specifically, philosophers, scientists, and educators have long debated whether human language (and human knowledge more broadly) depends on innate concepts or representations, a position historically associated with content nativism 1 (see Box 1).

Determining what, if anything, is innate matters not only for theories of language acquisition, but also for broader accounts of human cognition and of how biology and experience jointly shape development and evolution.

There is broad agreement that some features of the architecture of learning must themselves be biologically endowed (contra Locke, 1690/1948), such that even "the behaviorist is knowingly and cheerfully up to his neck in innate mechanisms" (Quine, 1969, pp.
Beyond this minimal commitment, however, consensus quickly breaks down.
Yet any complete theory of language acquisition must ultimately specify precisely what is innate, how it is represented, and how it interacts with experience during learning.

Within language acquisition research, innateness has historically catalyzed vigorous scientific debate that focused on whether humans are born with specialized cognitive structures for language (and/or thought), or whether linguistic representations instead emerge from domain-general learning mechanisms, potentially in combination with social interaction.

At one pole sit perspectives based on strong nativist frameworks, often based on theories of Chomsky (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?hvrMDv  Chomsky, 1965) and other scholars from this tradition (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?GYvJT8  Jackendoff, 2002 Jackendoff, , 2010;; Pinker, 1994).

text.text: Today, contemporary developmental science provides little support for treating the innate and acquired as opposing causal forces.

It is widely acknowledged that development arises through continuous interactions among organismic and environmental processes such that even strongly biologically prepared capacities depend on developmental environments for their realization (Griffiths & Tabery, 2013; Mameli & Bateson, 2011).

text.text: The traditional nature-nurture opposition is therefore a false dichotomy.

Moving away from a historical debate towards contemporary discourse, the literature now encompasses a wide range of alternative accounts to which we return below in considering contemporary proposals (e.g., Aslin & Newport, 2012; Hartshorne & Snedeker, 2026; Lake et al., 2017; Levinson, 2025;  see also Box 2).

text.text: Our goal is not to revive debates around nativism and empiricism, nor to replace this historical opposition with broad claims of interactionism.
Instead, we argue that agreement about interactionism does not eliminate the need to specify the interacting components and the nature of interactions.
The question of innateness, as we characterize it here, concerns the learner-internal component of how language is learned-an indispensable part of any interactionist account.

By describing innateness as an "orienting principle", we mean that it serves to organize our approach to explanation: what properties of the learner must be in place for language to emerge through interaction and over time?

This approach invites theories that specify the learner's contributions to language learning and that explore how these contributions interact with particular developmental environments to produce observed outcomes.
Innate specification could take very different forms.

They might include a broadly applicable statistical learning architecture, biases in attention or perception, early emerging sociocognitive capacities, conceptual primitives, or specifically linguistic representations (see Box 2).
These possibilities correspond to different tiers of explanation, and the evidence reviewed below bears differently on each.

Our aim is therefore not to establish that language is "innate" in a unitary sense, but to use contemporary evidence to prioritize precision and specificity in formulating plausible claims about what is developmentally prespecified and what can emerge through learning and interaction.

In this Perspective, we draw on three related but distinct bodies of evidence-linguistic and environmental diversity, language in human interaction, and language learning in artificial language models-to evaluate contemporary claims about innateness in language acquisition (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: In this Perspective, we draw on three related but distinct bodies of evidence-linguistic and environmental diversity, language in human interaction, and language learning in artificial language models-to evaluate contemporary claims about innateness in language acquisition (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: We focus on these developments because in combination, they constrain three fundamental components of any theory of language acquisition: the diversity of input and developmental outcomes that surface in learners' ecologies, how interactions mediate the relationship between input and outcomes, and the architectural constraints of a learning apparatus that produces human-like learning.

The progression of the paper thus moves from ecological descriptors of diverse conditions for learning, through interactional dynamics that structure learning within these diverse conditions, to candidate mechanisms for language learning.
Considered together, they invite testable questions about which biases, capacities, or representations must be developmentally prespecified and how the factors may interact with experience.
This Perspective is not intended as a comprehensive survey of the vast literature that is relevant to linguistic innateness.

Such a survey would encompass, among other topics, a more thorough accounting of comparative cognition (including non-human animals and artificial intelligence), theories and findings concerning language evolution (including homesign and emerging sign systems), the cultural amplification of learning biases, and research on behavioral genetics and heritability.

This article is intentionally put forth as a Perspective rather than a review article as its purpose is not to exhaustively catalogue the relevant evidence, but to selectively synthesize interconnected bodies of work that, when considered together, motivate new approaches to contemporary innateness.
This Perspective proceeds as follows.

First, we describe three complementary constraints on contemporary claims about innateness: Linguistic and environmental diversity establish the range of outcomes and learning environments that any theory must explain; research on human interaction clarifies what information is actually available to children within those environments and what capacities may be required to make use of it; and computational models provide a means of asking which properties of a learning system must be prespecified for human-like acquisition to emerge.

We then bring these directions together in the final section, where we consider how contemporary theories of innateness could be formulated and tested, and how the different proposals summarized in Box 2 locate prespecified structure at different levels.
Any account of linguistic innateness must grapple with two striking facts about human language.
The first is its remarkable consistency: across cultures, contexts, and circumstances, children reliably acquire language.
The second is its equally striking diversity: languages and contexts for learning vary profoundly, and children readily adapt to that variation.
Questions about the developmental origins of language are therefore inseparable from questions of diversity.

We begin with diversity because claims about innateness are often established from evidence of invariance: they propose that some property of the learner produces reliable developmental outcomes despite variation in experience.

Evaluating such claims therefore requires specifying which outcomes are consistent versus which vary, and whether apparent regularities survive examination across a sufficiently broad range of languages and learning environments.
We focus here on two forms of diversity: typological diversity, concerning the range of languages studied, and environmental diversity, concerning the range of learning ecologies considered.
Whereas typological diversity has long figured prominently in discourse on innateness, the challenges posed by environmental diversity have come into focus more recently.
Accounting for typological diversity has long been integral to any account of innate capacities that children bring to the task of acquiring language and remains a key consideration today.
At the outset, we provide a historical perspective with examples not intended to characterize the current state of theorizing which has evolved considerably since these proposals were formulated.

Rather, we cite these examples to guard against a historical simplification, the suggestion that traditional nativist accounts were largely indifferent to cross-linguistic diversity or developed without engaging variation across languages.

Linguistic diversity was often central to the nativist theoretical enterprise, both on the grounds that an innate architecture was required to accommodate diversity and as evidence used to distinguish between competing accounts of what that architecture might look like.

Theories within the Government and Binding framework, in particular, were designed to explain how children could rapidly acquire grammatical structures that vary across languages while drawing on an innate system (Baker, 2005; Chomsky, 1981a; Gibson & Wexler, 1994).

text.text: One dimension of typological diversity is structural diversity-that is, variation across languages in the grammatical categories, organizations, and constructions they instantiate.
Such variation places important constraints on claims about the linguistic content that could plausibly be innate.

Scholarly positions span a broad range, from proposals that learners are endowed with rich, high-level linguistic universals despite substantial cross-linguistic variation (e.g., Crain & Thornton, 1998; Pinker, 1984) to arguments that there are no true structural universals at all (Evans & Levinson, 2009), and that linguistic structure must instead be derived from variable input (see Ambridge et al., 2014; Braine, 1992; see also Section 3 below).

text.text: This range of positions remains central to contemporary debates about innateness because claims about innate contributions to language learning must ultimately be evaluated against the diversity of human languages that children learn.

The more systematically theories are tested across a broad range of language structures, the more clearly we can determine the extent to which proposed universals reflect species-wide constraints on language learning, distributional properties of particular languages, or interactions between the two.

A second, complementary constraint that has perhaps received less attention until recently comes from environmental diversity: the substantial variation across environments within which language learning outcomes are attained.

Children do not just acquire varying languages; they acquire language across contexts and communities that differ markedly in who speaks to children, how caregiving is networked and distributed, and how linguistic interaction is organized.

To the extent that language develops reliably across such heterogeneous learning ecologies, theories of language learning must account for both the stability of developmental outcomes across environmental variation and the ways in which learning is shaped by the particulars of that variation.
Paying closer attention to environmental variation complicates attempts to isolate the starting state of particular components of language from the experience through which they are acquired.

Because words must be learned from experience via exposure, classical nativist accounts often distinguished the lexicon from an autonomous syntactic system, with innateness claims focused primarily on the latter (e.g., Crain & Thornton, 1998; Pinker, 1984; Valian, 2014).

text.text: However, recent evidence, though not weakening the inescapable distinction between lexical and grammatical knowledge (speakers can clearly generalize grammatical patterns to novel or meaningless lexical items), presents a challenge to strong claims that lexical and grammatical knowledge are acquired through largely independent systems.
Evidence increasingly points to interdependence across these domains during development.

Across children, syntactic and morphological development are closely associated with vocabulary growth (Bates & Goodman, 1997; Frank et al., 2021), although the two remain empirically distinguishable (Donnelly et al., 2025).

text.text: Similarly, many contemporary computational models acquire lexical and structural regularities through shared learning mechanisms.
Neuroimaging studies have also not consistently identified a neural system devoted exclusively to syntax (e.g., Fedorenko, Ivanova, et al., 2024; Fedorenko, Piantadosi, et al., 2024).

text.text: Together, these findings are compatible with abstract grammatical representations but suggest that such representations may emerge through learning processes that are interdependent with lexical knowledge.

In line with this more integrated perspective, attention has shifted from diversity in syntactic structure alone to how children extract and build language structure, including but not limited to syntax, from the diverse inputs available to them in their environments.
Thus, environmental diversity is theoretically and empirically informative from both nativist and non-nativist perspectives.
In the search for what is innate, understanding environmental variation is especially important because it sheds light on how learning proceeds under diverse forms of input.

If children succeed despite substantially different forms of language input, then the mechanisms that have evolved to support language learning must be flexible enough to operate over such heterogeneous forms of experience.

Taken together, typological and environmental diversity define two interacting dimensions of the language-learning problem: children acquire different linguistic systems, and they do so across markedly different learning environments.
These dimensions are not independent.

The structure of the language being learned shapes which cues are available and informative, while the organization of the learning environment shapes how often those cues occur, how they are distributed, and how accessible they are to the learner (Elouatiq et al., 2026).

text.text: Systematic investigation of language variation is therefore essential for evaluating claims about what must be innate (see Goldin-Meadow, 2005).

text.text: At the same time, variation alone does not reveal which aspects of the available information children actually exploit in learning linguistic structure.

We therefore turn next to the structure of interaction, asking what information social interactions make available to learners and what learner-internal (or innate) capacities may be required to make use of it.

There is substantial and converging evidence illustrating that (a) children's social and linguistic input is rich in meaning and interactional in structure (e.g., Cameron-Faulkner, 2014; Chouinard & Clark, 2003; Clark & Kelly, 2022; Yu & Smith, 2017; Yurovsky et al., 2013), and (b) children have early-emerging capacities for social interaction that may help them adapt to and benefit from the interactional language environment in which they are being raised (e.g., Goren et al., 1975; Jaffe et al., 2001; Nguyen et al., 2022; Senju & Csibra, 2008).

text.text: Characterizing these interactions is important on the grounds that the strength of any argument for innate knowledge depends on knowledge of what information is available to the learner in connection with their emergent capabilities.
Any contemporary account of innateness must therefore take seriously what children's interactional environments provide and the internal capacities they bring to those environments.
The presence of structure in linguistic input does not, on its own, support any particular claim about innateness.
All theories of language development must explain how learners exploit the information available in their environments.
The relevance to innateness arises when we ask whether that information is sufficient to account for the knowledge children ultimately attain.

Traditional arguments for innate linguistic knowledge, such as Poverty of the Stimulus, have relied on claims about a gap between the evidence available in experience and the knowledge children ultimately attain (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?FEBJuL  Lasnik & Lidz, 2016, https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?FEBJuL.

text.text: Evaluating those claims therefore requires us to characterize the information available to learners in natural interaction.
We ask here whether interaction provides cues that narrow that gap and, in turn, what capacities learners must bring to exploit them.

To do this, we must first understand whether the affordances of interaction-however they are locally realized-give children access to the key information they need to make the right inductive generalizations about language.
The features of the input that matter must be considered given the diversity of socio-cultural environments sketched in section 2 above.
The first task, then, is to identify which aspects of language use help bridge the gap between the linguistic evidence children encounter and the knowledge they ultimately attain.

Because children encounter and acquire linguistic structures through communicating with others, audience design, intersubjectivity, and shared social aims are built into the very process of learning a language.

Thus, cross-cultural tendencies stemming from interactional needs can help us distinguish between languagespecific, social-specific, and other domains of innate support for robustness in early language learning.
It has long been suspected that these aspects of interaction can shed light on the process of learning itself.

For example, infant-directed speech (IDS)-a special case of audience design-has garnered a special explanatory role in theories of early language development as a mechanism for drawing infants' attention to linguistic signals and making the structure and meaning of those signals more salient, resulting in more efficient learning in some contexts (Cooper & Aslin, 1990; Fernald et al., 1989; Frank et al., 2009; Leung et al., 2021; ManyBabies Consortium, 2020; Moerk, 1976).

text.text: Thus, children encounter language as socially motivated, interactionally structured input that may guide attention to particular cues and engage adaptive learning strategies while also reflecting broader typological regularities in human language.

Sensitivity to these interactional cues, which ultimately arise from the need to understand others and make oneself understood, is built somehow into the learning process-the question is really what might be innate or linguistic about such sensitivities?

Computational linguistics research so far has done little to examine these questions -for example, by integrating multi-modal, interactive input and the sociocognitive skills that may support its use into model training.
Doing so may, however, shed critical light on key evolved features of human language acquisition, including adaptive learning and interactionready linguistic representations.

The next section examines what kinds of social sensitivities children might bring to the language learning task, innate or early emerging, to illustrate the routes by which sociocognitive abilities may shape the acquisition and transmission of linguistic representations.
Children appear to have the basic sociocognitive skills needed to coordinate and communicate with others from very early in life.

Theories accounting for these traits range from hypotheses about individual, human-specific capacities (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?5U9OHC  Gergely & Csibra, 2003; Tomasello, 2010 Tomasello, , 2014) ) to more general proposals linking social instincts to the emergence and transmission of linguistic systems (Levinson, 2006 (Levinson, , 2025)).

text.text: In sum, there is substantial evidence that early developing, universal sociocognitive skills combined with interactional linguistic input provides the fundamental context to support language learning across culturally and linguistically diverse developmental contexts.
This suggests an important new framing for our conceptions about what might be innate in human language acquisition.
We turn finally to language models (LMs) -artificial systems that process and produce text, made famous through commercial products such as ChatGPT and Claude.

LMs provide a new experimental tool in investigations of innateness, and their linguistic successes and shortcomings inform the identification of biases needed for human-like learning under developmentally realistic conditions.

Neural network models -which learn with relatively minimal innate content -have long been a source of challenges to content nativist theories of language acquisition (Elman et al., 1996; Rumelhart & McClelland, 1986).

In contrast, the advent -and widespread use -of neural network-based language models trained on vast quantities of data has substantially altered the discourse on innateness in development.

text.text: This argument only succeeds, however, if we are convinced that LMs do in fact learn target aspects of language correctly.
Despite flawless production, critics have asked whether LMs' underlying grammatical representations match those of humans.

Studies of models' internal representations suggest that hierarchical structures recognizable to linguists do in fact emerge from the operation of general learning mechanisms (Manning et al., 2020) -an instance of the general phenomenon of emergence (McClelland, 2010) -contra suggestions that such structures would have to be innately specified (Chomsky, 1981b).

text.text: In sum, LMs change the landscape of arguments about content nativism.

It is no longer possible to claim that specific aspects of language could not be learned without innate content on logical grounds; what remains open is whether they are learnable with the quantity and type of input that children receive, and whether children do in fact learn them.

Importantly, a model that reaches human-like performance without built-in linguistic content shows what can be learned in principle, not how children actually learn: it does not show that children lack innate structure, and these models carry architectural assumptions of their own.
These findings advance the field by focusing inquiry on the similarities and differences between LMs and human learners.
LMs provide a host of exciting opportunities to investigate visions of innateness beyond classical content nativism.

The preceding sections place substantial pressure on classical content nativism, while at the same time reinforcing the value of the fundamental question that motivated it.
Any theory in which linguistic structure emerges through learning must still specify which properties of the developing system must be already in place for that learning to occur.

Interactionism does not remove this requirement: explaining development requires characterizing not only the information available in the environment, but also which architectures, biases, capacities, or representations are developmentally prespecified and how they shape learning over time.
The three bodies of evidence reviewed above help make this question increasingly tractable, albeit in non-exhaustive ways.
Linguistic and environmental diversity constrain what prespecified capacities must be capable of accommodating across languages and environments.

Research on interaction constrains what information is actually available to, and sampled by, children and therefore what must be attributed to developmentally prespecified capacities rather than to the input alone.
Computational models provide a means of implementing and comparing candidate forms of prespecification and testing which are necessary for human-like learning.
Importantly, this does not imply a single form of innateness.

As summarized in Box 2, contemporary proposals about innateness locate prespecified structure at different levels: in a basic statistical learning architecture, in sociocognitive capacities, in conceptual primitives, or in specifically linguistic structure.
These alternatives make different claims about what must be present prior to or independently of linguistic learning and therefore place different explanatory burdens on experience.
Our aim in this section is to clarify how such claims can be made precise, mechanistic, and testable by providing four criteria (desiderata) for evaluating them (see also Figure 1).

text.text: First, modern theories must embrace and explain both typological and environmental variation.
Classical nativist theorizing took as its fundamental observations that language acquisition was essentially universal across typically developing children, but that language diversity was bounded.
These observations continue to be important guides to theory, but our understanding of both has broadened significantly.
The observation that language per se is universal is correct but masks the immense amount of variability between individual children (Frank et al., 2021; Kidd & Donnelly, 2020).

Second, viable theories must be precise and mechanistic in what they propose is innate, and why.

Our view, based partly on the evidence we have discussed here, is that future proposals for innateness will need to specify, at the very least, a prescribed basic statistical learning architecture (as proposed by minimal innateness theories), will probably need to include some basic sociocognitive biases to underpin the drive for interaction (sociocognitive innateness), and maybe even some semantic/conceptual primitives (conceptual innateness).

We are not yet convinced of the need to posit innate linguistic representations (the syntactic innateness of classical content nativism) to explain the data thus far, but we acknowledge that the evidence is not yet clear-cut and that our own views are affected by the preconceptions that we bring to this perspective.

A critical key leverage point for empirically adjudicating between different conceptions of innateness in the future will be the creation of larger, richer, datasets that document how children learn language in naturalistic contexts, and that identify the range of the sociocultural and linguistic contexts in which they learn.

Such data will enable us to build more mechanistic, formal models that can then be used to test competing hypotheses more precisely, by evaluating how closely models built with, and without, different sociocognitive, cognitive and syntactic primitives can simulate human language learning -in interaction, across cultures, and across languages.
These requirements are not individually new.
As mentioned earlier, generative theories have indeed sought to account for cross-linguistic variation, and computational approaches have long argued for explicit implementation.

However, a major challenge is to satisfy these constraints jointly, such that a proposal specifies what the learner contributes, specifies these contributions within a learning system, explicates how the system responds and adapts to developmentally relevant input, and evaluates whether it captures both consistency and variation in human learning.
Existing work provides positive examples of this approach.

Pearl and colleagues, for example, have examined whether phenomena traditionally attributed to innate grammatical constraints can be acquired by learners with explicitly specified representations and biases operating over realistic input (Pearl & Sprouse, 2013).

Taken together, these examples illustrate how contemporary approaches can move beyond broad claims about innateness by specifying, formalizing, and testing the particular learner constraints that shape acquisition in interaction with experience.
In this piece we have revisited the question of linguistic innateness in the light of a set of striking empirical developments that have emerged in the last one to two decades.
The first is the renewed interest in understanding language acquisition across languages, coupled with renewed appreciation for the extent of variation across individuals and contexts.

This development has widened the scope of inquiry beyond a small number of well-studied languages and populations, and with it has come a clearer recognition that language learning unfolds under highly diverse structural and social conditions.

The second is the greater emphasis on the interactional richness that underlies linguistic communication and on the study of interaction as an important site of discovery about the origins of language.

And the final development is the rise of LMs, which has offered a powerful new perspective on classic questions about the sources of linguistic structure, the relationship between input and learning, and the extent to which complex and seemingly language-like knowledge can emerge from learning algorithms operating over extensive input.
Each of these developments poses a challenge to traditional content nativist views that have argued that the universal acquisition of language must be driven by specific innate syntactic machinery.

As these empirical, technological, and methodological developments reshape our understanding of the origins of language, it is reasonable to query the place of innateness as a core theoretical construct.
We argue that its continuing value lies in directing attention to identifying which particular properties must be developmentally prespecified for language learning to proceed as it does.
The evidence reviewed here helps to focus that endeavor.
Linguistic and environmental diversity constrain the range of outcomes and environments that candidate forms of pre-specification must accommodate.
Research on interaction clarifies what information is actually available for children to sample, thereby refining claims about what must be prespecified rather than learned from experience.
Computational models offer an increasingly powerful means of implementing and comparing candidate architectures, biases, capacities, or representations.

Innateness therefore remains useful as an orienting principle not because it directly answers how language develops, but because it identifies a set of questions that contemporary theories must address.

The future of research on innateness in language lies in formulating and testing increasingly precise hypotheses about what is prespecified, in what form, and how those initial properties interact with experience over development.
The concept of innateness has a centuries-long history.
Classical philosophers such as Plato argued that some knowledge is inborn, while early modern thinkers such as René Descartes also defended the existence of innate ideas.

In contrast, seventeenth-and eighteenth-century philosophers such as John Locke and Immanuel Kant famously debated the origins of ideas in different ways, with Locke portraying the mind as a tabula rasa shaped by experience and Kant proposing that the mind contributes to organizing structures that make experience possible.
In the nineteenth century, Charles Darwin's theory of evolution reframed these questions by situating human cognition within a biological and comparative framework.

In the twentieth century, ethologists such as Niko Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz, developmental theorists such as Jean Piaget, and linguists such as Noam Chomsky each reshaped debates about what aspects of mind and behavior are biologically prepared versus constructed through experience.
Chomsky, in particular, placed human language at the center of the modern debate, proposing that language acquisition rests on innate linguistic knowledge in the form of syntactic structures.

Since Chomsky's foundational proposal, debates over the origins and mechanisms of language learning have led to the development of competing frameworks, including parameter-setting theories, minimalist theories, and Words and Rules approaches associated with scholars such as Steven Pinker, on one side, and usage-based approaches, social-interactionist theories, and connectionist models, often associated with theorists such as Michael Tomasello, on the other.

More recent work by researchers such as Elizabeth Spelke and Susan Carey has further extended the debate by examining whether infants begin life with core systems of knowledge that structure subsequent learning.
These perspectives on what is innate variably align with nativist or empiricist orientations and have generally sought to classify language as a product of nativism, constructivism, or empiricism.

The research literature contains a variety of more modern instantiations of innateness, that roughly fall into four different frameworks, which we review, and then briefly compare in the table below to the desiderata described in section 5.

The most minimal form of innateness is that only a basic statistical learning architecture is prespecified in learners and the rest of language stems from the operation of this powerful learning mechanism in rich interactional contexts.
Indeed, statistical learning accounts of early language acquisition often describe these abilities as "innate learning mechanisms" (Aslin & Newport, 2012).

Several prominent theoretical frameworks focus on the importance of social cognition.
From an evolutionary perspective, there is increasing evidence for the adaptation of human social coordination and mind-reading abilities relative to other primates (Tomasello, 2020).

text.text: Perhaps linguistic structures are not innately specified, but rather are built on innate non-linguistic conceptual primitives.
On this sort of proposal, relatively little about language is prespecified per se, but structures in language emerge from a mapping between the child's ontology and the language they hear.

The classic "semantic bootstrapping" proposal includes both innate syntactic and semantic elements, as well as specified mappings between these (Pinker, 1984). Hartshorne & Snedeker (2026) update this proposal based on the idea that a "clean mapping" between innate conceptual structures and language is all that is needed to kick-start language learning.
